rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shacāʾir is the plural of shacīra, from a pattern meaning marked; ishʿār is informing through sensation, and shaʿr is sensory knowledge.
rows.anchor: الشعائر واحدتها: شعيرة، وهي فعيلة بمعنى مفعلة، والمشعرة: المعلمة، والإشعار: الإعلام من طريق الإحساس، والشعر: العلم من طريق الحس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anything made known or marked as a sign for something may be called a shaʿīra.
rows.anchor: كل شيء جعل علما على شيء، أو أعلم بعلامة جاز أن يسمى شعيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Offerings brought to Mecca are called divine signs because they are marked with blood; al-Kumayt's verse uses the term for sacrificial victims by which people draw near.
rows.anchor: والهدي التي تهدى إلى مكة تسمى شعائر؛ لأنها مشعرة بالدم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In a report through ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥuṭaym ibn Ḍubayʿa stole camels from the Prophet's pasture, then marked and offered them; when Muslims pursued the Yamama pilgrims, this verse prohibited violating even marked offerings belonging to non-Muslims.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: أن (الحطيم بن ضبيعة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda defines shacāʾir in Arabic usage as offerings marked for sacrifice.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: الشعائر في كلام العرب: الهدايا المشعرة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj defines them as things marked or designated to be offered to the Sacred House.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: هي ما أشعر، أي أعلم ليهدى إلى بيت الله الحرام

rows.speaker: جماعة من أهل المعاني
rows.claim: A group of semanticists understands shacāʾir as all worship rites Allah designated as signs for people.
rows.anchor: وقال جماعة: هي جميع متعبدات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid identify the shacāʾir as the rites of pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومجاهد: هي مناسك الحج

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسلم
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim says they are anything made a sign of obedience to Allah.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن مسلم: هي كل شيء جعل علما من أعلام طاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs and landmarks of pilgrimage include Ṣafā, Marwa, the stations for entering consecration, and ʿArafāt; if the term means offerings, the prohibition bars plunder, and if it means rites, it bars transgression, neglect, and falling short.
rows.anchor: فالشعائر: العلامات والمعالم للحج نحو الصفا والمروة والمواقيت وعرفة وما أشبهها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says Arabs generally did not count Ṣafā and Marwa among pilgrimage rites or walk between them, so the command forbids treating that omission as permissible.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: كانت عامة العرب لا يرون الصفا والمروة من شعائر الحج، ولا يطوفون بينهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the verse forbids abandoning any commanded rite: circumambulation, saʿy, touching the Corner, the departures from ʿArafāt and Muzdalifa, and stoning the pillars; Arabs disputed whether Ṣafā, Marwa, and ʿArafāt were rites.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو صالح عن ابن عباس: يقول: لا تستحلوا شيئا من ترك المناسك كلها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In another report, polytheists performed pilgrimage, offered sacrifices, honored the sacred stations, and traded there; Muslims wished to raid them, so the verse restrained them.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية أخرى: كان المشركون يحجون البيت الحرام، ويهدون الهدايا، ويعظمون حرمة المشاعر

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī interprets the command as forbidding treating the abandonment of any pilgrimage rite as permissible.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: أي لا تستحلوا ترك شيء من المناسك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpret the verse as forbidding passing the pilgrimage boundary without entering consecration.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن هذا ورد في النهي عن مجاوزة الميقات بغير إحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boundary interpretation fits the wording if shacāʾir means landmarks, since the pilgrimage boundaries are among Allah's signs.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى يحتمله اللفظ؛ لأن تقدير الآية على القول الذي يقول: إن الشعائر المعالم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda explain not violating the sacred month as not fighting in it.
rows.anchor: بالقتال فيه. عن ابن عباس (¬1) وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hady means a camel, cow, or sheep offered to the House; hadiyya is its singular and hady its plural, as a cited poem illustrates.
rows.anchor: الهدي ما أهدي إلى بيت الله تعالى من ناقة وبقرة أو شاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qalāʾid is the plural of qalāda, anything placed around a person's, camel's, or dog's neck.
rows.anchor: هي جمع قلادة، وهي: ما جعل في العنق، سواء جعل في عنق الإنسان أو البدنة أو الكلب

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes take qalāʾid to mean collared offerings, with the possessive word omitted; the phrase may mean offerings both collared and uncollared, or non-offerings collared for safety.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في تفسير القلائد ههنا، فقال أكثر المفسرين: هي الهدايا المقلدة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says not to obstruct offerings or frighten people who have collared their camels; this reads qalāʾid as their owners, again with a possessive omitted.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: يقول لا تعترضوا الهدي ولا تخيفوا من قلد بعيره

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes describe constant pre-Islamic tribal warfare except in sacred months; marked camels, people driving offerings, travelers wearing sanctuary bark, and pilgrims in ʿumra were also left safe. Muslims were told to preserve this security temporarily for public benefit until abrogation.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: كانت الحرب في الجاهلية قائمة بين العرب طول الدهر، يتغاورون ويتناهبون إلا في الأشهر الحرم

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says fearful travelers or people pursued for blood revenge wore bark from sanctuary trees, and similarly collared camels, so enemies would not attack them; breaking this convention brought blame, as a poem about killing two such men shows.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: إن الرجل من العرب كان إذا خاف على نفسه عدوا، أو مطالبا بثأر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poem's al-liḥāʾ means bark from the trees of the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: يريد باللحاء: شجر الحرم

rows.speaker: مطرف بن الشخير وعطاء
rows.claim: Muṭarrif ibn al-Shikhkhīr and ʿAṭāʾ take qalāʾid literally: polytheists wore and collared themselves with bark from Meccan trees for safety, and the verse forbids taking the trees to make such collars.
rows.anchor: وقال مطرف بن الشخير (¬4) وعطاء: أراد بالقلائد نفس القلائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first interpretation, that qalāʾid means collared offerings or their owners, is the apparent reading and was chosen by al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj.
rows.anchor: والظاهر القول الأول، وهو اختيار الفراء والزجاج

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says travelers outside sacred months collared camels to secure safe passage; Meccans used bark, while other Arabs used wool or hair.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: كانت العرب إذا أرادت أن تسافر في غير الأشهر الحرم قلد أحدهم بعيره

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ interprets those intending the Sacred House as people who go to it or intend it, including polytheists.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: يقول: ولا تمنعوا من أم البيت الحرام أو أراده من المشركين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the favor sought by pilgrims as trade.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد التجارة

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar specifies the favor as profit from trade.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عمر: الربح في التجارة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says pilgrims seek to please Allah through their pilgrimage; in a report through ʿAṭāʾ, the phrase applies even if they are polytheists.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني: أنهم يترضون الله بحجهم

rows.speaker: أهل العلم
rows.claim: Scholars say polytheists intended to seek Allah's pleasure through pilgrimage, though they would not attain it; that intention could still confer a degree of inviolability.
rows.anchor: قال أهل العلم: إن المشركين كانوا يقصدون بحجهم ابتغاء رضوان الله

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Semanticists understand the pleasure as what the polytheists claimed or imagined, since unbelievers cannot attain it; the ironic wording resembles Qur'anic address in Ṭā Hā 20:97 and al-Dukhān 44:49.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: معنى قوله: {ورضوانا} أى: على زعمهم وفيما يظنون

rows.speaker: زهرة اليمن
rows.claim: Zahra al-Yaman's taunt to Jarīr exemplifies Arabs' reported speech that presents a claim as the speaker's own.
rows.anchor: قال زهرة اليمن (¬3) يهجو جريرا: أبلغ كليبا وأبلغ عنك شاعرها

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarīr replies to Zahra al-Yaman in a verse that likewise illustrates this reported form of speech.
rows.anchor: وقال جرير: ألم يكن في وسوم قد وسمت بها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Most scholars, including Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatāda, say the passage through this phrase was abrogated by the command to kill polytheists wherever found.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل العلم
rows.claim: Most scholars say the verse was abrogated by both the command to kill polytheists and the ban on their approaching the Sacred Mosque, so polytheists may not perform pilgrimage or claim protection through sacred months, offerings, collars, or pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وأكثر أهل العلم قالوا: نسخت هذه الآية قوله تعالى: {فاقتلوا المشركين حيث وجدتموهم}

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī says only one verse in al-Māʾida was abrogated: this command not to violate Allah's signs.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: لم ينسخ من المائدة إلا آية واحدة

rows.speaker: جماعة
rows.claim: Another group holds that nothing in this sūra is abrogated and that the verse remains operative.
rows.anchor: وذهب جماعة إلى أنه لا منسوخ في هذه السورة، وأن هذه الآية محكمة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Abū Bakr Ibn al-Anbārī argues for an operative reading: Muslims must not frighten their own fellow believers going to the House, the sacred month is specially honored, offerings must reach their destination, and collars protect sanctuary-seekers.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر ابن الأنباري: فمن ذهب إلى أن هذه الآية محكمة قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After reporting Ibn al-Anbārī's reasoning, the author says the majority position is the apparent one.
rows.anchor: هذا كلامه (1)، والظاهر ما عليه الجمهور

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains the command to hunt after leaving consecration as permission, not an obligation; it lifts the earlier prohibition, like the command to disperse after Friday prayer or an instruction to enter after paying.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: هذا لفظ أمر، معناه الإباحة؛ لأن الله عز وجل حرم الصيد على المحرم

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī derives jarama as the verbal noun of an agent who brings evil upon himself and his people.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأعرابي: الجرم مصدر الجارم الذي يجرم نفسه وقومه شرا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes gloss the phrase as do not let hatred of a people lead you to act; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda, along with al-Kisāʾī and Yūnus, give this interpretation.
rows.anchor: والمفسرون يقولون في هذا: لا يحملنكم بغض قوم

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās gives جرمني زيد على بغضك as an expression meaning that Zayd made or caused me to hate you.
rows.anchor: قال أبو العباس: يقال: جرمني زيد على بغضك، أي: حملني عليه

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل اللغة والمعاني
rows.claim: Most linguists and semanticists take the verb to mean do not make yourselves acquire or incur wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وأكثر أهل اللغة والمعاني يقولون: لا يكسبنكم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ cites Arab expressions for a family's provider and one who earns for his family, and glosses the verse as do not let hatred of a people earn you aggression.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: سمعت العرب تقول (¬1): فلان جريمة أهله، وخرج يجرم أهله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the cited line about Fazāra, Fazāra is accusative: the wound caused them to acquire anger, demonstrating jarama in the sense of earning.
rows.anchor: المعنى: جرمتهم الطعنة الغضب، أي: أكسبتهم

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī gives the same acquire meaning for يجرمنكم and cites a poem where someone's hands earned the punishment described.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك قال ابن الأنباري في: {يجرمنكم}، وأنشد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī analyzes يجرمنكم as a two-object verb meaning make you acquire, parallel to يكسبنكم.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: تأويل: {لا يجرمنكم} يكسبنكم، وهو فعل متعد إلى مفعولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase جريمة ناهض, describing an eagle, can mean one that earns food for a fledgling or, without an omitted possessive, a fledgling's provider; jarama can mean earning or effort that accrues to its agent, while ajrama is used for committing sin.
rows.anchor: وأما قول الشاعر في صفة عقاب: جريمة ناهض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command means do not let hatred for a people cause you to acquire or commit aggression.
rows.anchor: ومعنى {ولا يجرمنكم شنآن قوم} لا تكتسبوا لبغض قوم عدوانا ولا تقترفوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition is grammatically directed at hatred or discord but addresses the listeners: they are the first object and aggression the second; the same construction appears in Āl ʿImrān 3:102 and Hūd 11:89.
rows.anchor: ولفظ النهي واقع على الشنآن، والمعنى بالنهي المخاطبون

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd gives several forms of the verb shaniʾa, all meaning to hate someone.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد: شنئت الرجل أشنؤه شنأ، وشنآنا، وشنأ، ومشنأة

rows.speaker: الفراء وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿAmr also report shanaʾ with a kasra on the nūn.
rows.anchor: وزاد الفراء وأبو عمرو: شنأ، بالكسر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda reports shanānan with a vowelless nūn.
rows.anchor: وأبو عبيدة: شنآنا بالجزم

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abū al-Haytham reports the forms shanʾa and mashnaʾan.
rows.anchor: وأبو الهيثم: شنأة، ومشنئا

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd says shanʾān for a man and shanʾāna for a woman are declinable, though the masculine may be treated as diptote because its feminine is shanʾā; faʿlān is both an uncommon adjective pattern and verbal-noun pattern, with examples including liyān and Abū ʿUbayda's shanʾān.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو زيد: رجل شنآن، وامرأة شنآنة، مصروفان

rows.speaker: الأحوص
rows.claim: Al-Aḥwaṣ's verse uses the expression dhū al-shanān as poetic evidence for the word's form and meaning.
rows.anchor: وأنشد للأحوص (¬6): وإن عاب فيه ذو الشنان وفندا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem's dhū al-shanān reflects the regular easing of hamza: delete the hamza and move its vowel to the preceding letter, as in easing ẓamʾān and malʾān.
rows.anchor: قوله: (ذو الشنان) على التخفيف القياسي، كقولك في تخفيف ظمآن، وملآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective pattern faʿlān is uncommon when it has no feminine faʿlā, as with shayḥān.
rows.anchor: وأما فعلان في الوصف فليس بالكثير إذا لم يكن له فعلى، ومن ذلك: شيحان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿlān is also a verbal-noun pattern, illustrated by naqazān, nagharān, ghalayān, nafayān, and ghathayān; shanʾān belongs to this group.
rows.anchor: فالمصدر كالنقزان، والنغران، والغليان، والنفيان، والغثيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿlān adjectives include zafiyān, ṣamiyān, and qaṭwān, the last describing short steps; al-Aṣmaʿī's verse supplies another example.
rows.anchor: والوصف نحو: الزفيان، والصميان، والقطوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poem places a past negation about birth in a conditional clause, showing that a past act can represent the possibility of a similar event.
rows.anchor: إذا ما انتسبنا لم تلدني لئيمة

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd cites a poem using al-abyān as further evidence for the adjective pattern.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو زيد: وقبلك ما هاب الرجال ظلامعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some faʿlān forms are nouns rather than adjectives, including warshan and al-ʿaljān, a tooth-cleaning shrub.
rows.anchor: وقد يجيء الاسم الذي لا يكون صفة على فعلان نحو: الورشان، والعلجان

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most reciters read shanʾān on the faʿlān pattern because it is a common verbal-noun pattern; those who leave the nūn vowelless also have verbal-noun precedent, so the readings have the same meaning.
rows.anchor: واختلف القراء في هذا الحرف، فالأكثرون قرءوا على: فعلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse means that hatred of a people for barring you should not make you aggress; the verbal noun is annexed to its object with its agent omitted, as in two other Qur'anic constructions.
rows.anchor: وإذا كان كذلك فالمعنى في القراءتين واحد وإن اختلف اللفظان

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن كثير
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read the hamza in an ṣaddūkum with kasra; the other readers use fatḥa.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في قوله: {أن صدوكم} فقرأ أبو عمرو وابن كثير بكسر الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra makes an conditional: although the barring at Ḥudaybiyya is past, it stands for any like future event; the preceding prohibition supplies the response, meaning if they bar you, do not acquire aggression.
rows.anchor: وحجة من كسر الهمزة أنه جعل (أن) للجزاء وإن كان الصد ماضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the kasra reading, the response to the conditional is supplied by لا يجرمنكم: if a people bar you from the Sacred Mosque, do not incur aggression.
rows.anchor: وجواب (إن) قد أعنى عنه ما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa, the first أن is causal and the second أن تعتدوا is the second object of the verb.
rows.anchor: وهو أنه مفعول له، التقدير: لا يجرمنكم شنآن قوم؛ لأن صدوكم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says Muslims must not let hatred of Meccan disbelievers who barred them at Ḥudaybiyya lead them to aggress against Yamama pilgrims, legalize what is forbidden, block their mosque access, or attack their offerings.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل في قوله تعالى: {ولا يجرمنكم شنآن} الآية: يقول لا يحملنكم بغض كفار مكة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ glosses cooperation in righteousness and piety as helping one another.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: ليعن بعضكم بعضا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the command is jussive because it is an imperative and is not coordinated with تعتدوا.
rows.anchor: وهو في موضع جزم؛ لأنه أمر وليس بمعطوف على (تعتدوا)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says everything earlier in the verse was abrogated except Muslims' cooperation in righteousness and piety.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: ما مضى من هذه الآية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines righteousness as what Allah commanded and piety as leaving what He forbade; Abū al-ʿĀliya gives a similar explanation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: {وتعاونوا على البر والتقوى} وهو ما أمرت به

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says righteousness and piety comprise everything in which Allah has pleasure.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء في البر والتقوى: يريد كل ما كان لله فيه

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ interprets sin and aggression as disobedience to Allah and transgressing His limits.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء: يريد معاصي الله والتعدي في حدوده

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil explains fear Allah as not treating anything forbidden as lawful, and says Allah is severe when He punishes.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل ثم حذرهم فقال: {واتقوا الله} فلا تستحلوا محرما

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Zayd al-Khayl asked the Prophet about game caught by their dogs and falcons, since carrion was forbidden; this verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: إن عدي بن حاتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mādhā can be parsed as a single noun in the nominative, with uḥilla as its predicate; alternatively, mā alone is the noun and dhā is the predicate, with uḥilla as a relative clause, meaning what thing was made lawful.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {ماذا} إن جعلته اسما فهو رفع بالابتداء وخبره (أحل)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the permitted good things as all lawful things.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد من جميع الحلال

rows.speaker: أهل العلم
rows.claim: Scholars say Arabs avoided many things they found repulsive and ate what they enjoyed; Allah permitted what they liked unless revelation prohibited it, including livestock, lizards, jerboas, and rabbits. They treat this as a broad rule: animals Arabs find pleasant are lawful and those they find repugnant are forbidden, in line with al-Aʿrāf 7:157.
rows.anchor: قال أهل العلم: كانت العرب تستقذر أشياء كثيرة فلا تأكلها، وتستطيب أشياء فتأكلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭayyib can mean pleasing or tasty; permitted lawful food is also called good by analogy because both tasty and lawful food are free of harm.
rows.anchor: والطيب في اللغة: المستلذ، والحلال المأذون فيه، يسمى أيضا طيبا

rows.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Muqātil and al-Kalbī interpret the good things as slaughtered animals.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل والكلبي: المراد بالطيبات الذبائح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the broad interpretation of all good lawful things because it covers more and is held by most scholars.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أولى؛ لأنه أعم في التحليل، وعليه أكثر العلماء

rows.speaker: الزجاج وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and other scholars understand an omitted word, game: and [game] from trained hunting animals; the next clause about eating what they hold and the question about hunting support the ellipsis, a view shared by all semanticists.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج وغيره: يريد: وصيد ما علمتم من الجوارح، فحذف الصيد وهو مراد في الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, وما علمتم can start a new sentence whose predicate is eat what they hold, yielding sound wording without ellipsis.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يقال: قوله تعالى: {وما علمتم} ابتداء كلام وخبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jawāriḥ are hunting birds and predatory beasts that acquire prey; the singular is jāriḥa, and a hunting dog counts as one because the root means to earn.
rows.anchor: وأما الجوارح: فهي الكواسب من الطير والسباع ذوات الصيد، والواحدة جارحة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAṭāʾ includes hunting birds, dogs, cheetahs, lynxes, raptors such as the falcon and hawk, eagles, and the zamaj; prey killed by these hunters is lawful.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: يريد الطير تصيد، والكلاب، والفهود

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Layth reports that Mujāhid counted falcons, hawks, cheetahs, and other hunting beasts among the jawāriḥ.
rows.anchor: سئل مجاهد عن الصقر والبازي والفهد

rows.speaker: ابن عمر والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar and al-Ḍaḥḥāk restrict jawāriḥ to dogs and require live prey caught by other animals to be ritually slaughtered; a similar view is related from al-Suddī.
rows.anchor: ابن عمر (¬7) والضحاك أنهما قالا: الجوارح الكلاب دون غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the dog-only view is not acted upon.
rows.anchor: وهو قول غير معمول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukallib is someone who trains dogs to catch game, and a hunter is called mukallib because he trains the dog; a poem illustrates the term.
rows.anchor: المكلب: الذي يعلم الكلاب أخذ الصيد، ويقال للصائد مكلب

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Semanticists say mukallibīn does not prove that only dogs are permitted for hunting, just as calling someone a trainer does not limit the thing trained.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: وليس في قوله: (مكلبين) دليل على أنه إنما أبيح صيد الكلاب خاصة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the hunters train the animals to seek prey and not eat it, just as Allah taught people.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: تؤدبونهن (¬4) لطلب الصيد

rows.speaker: العلماء
rows.claim: Scholars define a trained dog as one that obeys when released and urged on, holds rather than eats its catch, answers its call, and does not flee when approached; repeated behavior establishes training.
rows.anchor: قال العلماء: وصفة الكلب المعلم الذي يحل صيده هو أن يكون إذا أرسله صاحبه

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: Grammarians take min in مما as partitive: only the meat, not offal or blood, is eaten.
rows.anchor: دخلت (من) في قوله (مما) للتبعيض؛ لأنه إنما أحل أكل بعضه

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says min is extra here, so the meaning is eat what the animals held.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: من ههنا زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another grammarian rejects the extra-min reading because min is only extra in negation and questions; in 2:271 it instead marks the source, meaning Allah covers deeds the people want hidden among their sins.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: هذا خطأ؛ لأن من لا تزاد في الواجب

rows.speaker: العلماء
rows.claim: If a trained dog wounds and kills prey that the hunter finds dead, it is lawful because the hunter's wound counts as slaughter; the same applies to other trained hunters, arrows, spears, and pointed shafts that wound.
rows.anchor: قال العلماء: إذا كان الضاري وهو الكلب معلما كما وصفنا، ثم صاد صيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a broadhead kills by its flat side without wounding and the prey is not caught alive for slaughter, it is forbidden.
rows.anchor: فإن أصابه المعراض بعرضه (فقتله ولم تدرك (¬4)) ذكاته فهو حرام

rows.speaker: كثير من العلماء
rows.claim: Many scholars forbid prey a dog smothers by pinning it down without a wound, but the author says analogy permits it because the dog held it for its owner; returning prey unharmed can better show training, which need not involve wounding.
rows.anchor: لم يجز أكله عند كثير من العلماء، والقياس أنه حلال؛ لأنه مما أمسكه على صاحبه

rows.speaker: الكلبي وغيره من المفسرين
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and other exegetes say to mention Allah when releasing the hunting dogs.
rows.anchor: يعني إذا أرسلتم الكلاب. قال الكلبي وغيره من المفسرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAṭāʾ says to say Allah's name at release; forgetting does not prevent eating, and he connects the believer's and Muslim's names with Allah's names al-Muʾmin and al-Salām.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: {واذكروا اسم الله عليه} إذا أطلقت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan permits eating when a believer forgets the basmala at release, since Allah's name is part of his religion, like the knife he uses if he forgets to name Allah at slaughter.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: إذا أرسل المؤمن كلبه

rows.speaker: العلماء
rows.claim: Scholars say it is preferable to slaughter or release hunting animals in Allah's name; if the name is omitted, the meat remains lawful according to a prophetic report that a believer slaughters in Allah's name whether he names Him or not, explaining Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan.
rows.anchor: قال العلماء: الأولى الذبح علي اسم الله، وإرسال الجوارح على اسم الله

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha asked about game brought by Bedouins when it was unknown whether Allah's name had been said; the Prophet told them to say it themselves and eat.
rows.anchor: وقالت عائشة لرسول الله

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Semanticists say the pronoun in عليه refers to the act of releasing the animal, though release is not explicitly mentioned, because context makes it clear.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: الهاء في قوله: (عليه) تعود إلى الإرسال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This answers the Jews' claim that they knew no religion worse than Islam: the Prophet is told to ask whether he should inform them of a worse recompense than what they censured in Muslim belief.
rows.anchor: هذا جواب لليهود حين قالوا: ما نعرف دينا شرا من دينكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, worse may refer to the Muslims whom the Jews maligned.
rows.anchor: وقيل: شر من الذين طعنتم عليهم من المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathūba is accusative as a specification and follows the pattern mafʿūla, like maqūla and majūra; it is a verbal noun, as are maʿqūl and maysūr, though another view derives it on mafʿila like makrama.
rows.anchor: ووزنها: مفعولة، كقولك: مقولة، ومجورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min may be genitive in apposition to shar, giving the meaning inform you about one whom Allah cursed.
rows.anchor: (من) يجوز أن يكون في موضع خفض بدلا من

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows min as a nominative independent clause; al-Zajjāj explains the case by an implicit huwa, as in the statement in al-Ḥajj 22:72 that the Fire is worse.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون رفعا بالاستئناف. قاله الفراء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ also allows min as a direct object of inform, by analogy with informing someone of a report or of Zayd standing, but prefers the genitive analysis.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: لو نصبت (من) بوقوع الإنباء عليه، كما تقول: أنبأتك خبرا
